cues.text: Let's turn to chapter six: failure management and architecture design.
Start with the overall recipe the source gives for coping with failure.
Use redundancy across independent failure domains.
That means you keep more than one copy of your data and your services, and you place those copies so that a single cause cannot take them all down together.
A failure domain is simply the set of things that fail together, for example one server, one rack, one data centre, or one region.
Next, the replication that keeps those copies in step must be monitored, so you notice when a copy falls behind or breaks.
Failover, which is switching to a standby when the main node fails, should be automated but fenced.
Automated means a person does not have to wake up and press a button.
Fenced means the old node is actively prevented from carrying on acting as if it were still in charge.
On top of this, you keep backups, and, importantly, you test recovery, because a backup you have never restored is only a hope.
Now to the danger that fencing guards against.
Split brain occurs when competing nodes believe they can act as leader.
Imagine a network fault that separates two nodes.
Each cannot see the other, so each decides it must take over.
Now two leaders accept writes that conflict.
The source's remedy is quorum and fencing.
A quorum means a decision needs agreement from a majority of the nodes, so only one side of a split can ever have the majority.
Fencing shuts out the other side.
Together, quorum and fencing prevent conflicting authoritative writes, meaning two different versions of the truth being accepted at once.
Two measures describe how well you recover.
RTO, the recovery time objective, is the target recovery duration: how long the system may be down before it must be working again.
RPO, the recovery point objective, is the tolerable data loss measured in time.
For example, an RPO of five minutes would mean you can accept losing up to the last five minutes of changes.
That five-minute figure is only my illustration, not from the source.
Remember it this way: RTO is about how long you are down, and RPO is about how much recent data you can afford to lose.
The source then names a trade-off.
Strong cross-region writes improve coordination, because every region agrees before a write is accepted.
But they increase network latency, since the write must travel between distant regions and wait for answers.
Caching and local reads may help reduce that delay, but only when staleness is acceptable.
Staleness means the data a reader sees might be slightly out of date.
So if your application cannot tolerate old data, these shortcuts are not available to you.
The last block moves to distributed queries.
A cross-shard join can require remote data transfer.
A shard is one partition of a database, held on one node.
When a join needs rows from two shards, one shard may have to send its data across the network to the other, and that is expensive.
The source gives several ways to reduce the cost.
Push predicates and projections near the data.
A predicate is a filter condition, and a projection chooses only the columns you need.
Applying both where the data lives means less data has to travel.
Colocate related data, which means storing rows that are often joined together on the same node.
Use local indexes, so each node can find its own rows quickly.
And avoid unnecessary transfers altogether.
Finally, data localisation restricts where data can reside under applicable rules.
These might be legal or regulatory requirements about the location of data.
The source adds one important point: replicas and backups are part of the design.
So when you decide where data may live, you must include every copy, not just the primary one.
A backup or replica placed in the wrong location would break the rule just as surely as the main database would.
